sections.h2: What a North Carolina seller pays at closing
sections.html:
Expect four recurring costs on the seller side: deed excise tax, loan payoff, attorney fees, and filing charges for any paper you must record. Your total turns on the contract, so go through the attorney's settlement statement one line at a time.

Some charges are set by statute and others are bargained over in the sales contract. We stick here to the ones the General Statutes spell out, since they stay the same from one closing to the next.

  • The deed excise tax, which falls on the seller by law.
  • Paying off the mortgage or deed of trust, and getting that lien cleared from the record.
  • The closing attorney's fee for the deed and title review.
  • Register of deeds charges for any document you must record.
  • The year's county property tax bill, which runs on its own due date and interest schedule.

Agent commission, repair credits and the like come from your contract rather than the statutes. Get each of them in writing from the listing agent or the attorney before you sign.

sections.h2: Why a home sale needs an attorney
sections.html:
Under G.S. 84-2.1, drafting a deed or passing upon a title is legal work, so a lawyer has to do it. The definition names deeds, mortgages and title abstracting.

Brokers may fill in a preprinted form under that statute, and anyone may complete a preprinted residential lease, but nobody without a law license may prepare a contract or deed conveying North Carolina real property for someone else. So closings here happen at law offices.

Pick the closing lawyer early, or at least approve who does the work. This lawyer checks the title history, collects the payoff number, writes the deed, and makes sure the deed tax and filing charge get to the county. If a cash buyer chooses the lawyer, you can still ask to see a draft settlement statement early.

sections.h2: The excise tax as a seller cost
sections.html:
The seller owes it. G.S. 105-228.30 sets a rate of $1 per $500 of price or value, rounding any remainder up, and the transferor must pay before the deed is filed.

Because it tracks the price, this is frequently the largest line item the statutes assign to a seller. Expect your lawyer to deduct it from what you net and send it in with the deed. A tract that crosses a county line goes to the county with the greater value.

See our excise tax page for exempt transfers and how the money is split.

One schedule in G.S. 161-10 applies in every county. The register of deeds collects up front, and the statute says no other fees may be added.

Recording fees under G.S. 161-10
Document or serviceFee
Standard instrument, first 15 pages$26.00 plus $4.00 for each added page
Satisfaction or cancellation of a loan lienFree
Nonstandard format$25.00 surcharge
Each extra instrument within one document$10.00

Your deed sits in the first row. The buyer's lender pays the separate, higher schedule for a mortgage or deed of trust, so that charge rarely shows up on a seller's statement.

sections.h2: Mortgage payoff and the recorded lien
sections.html:
When the loan is paid off, the lender has 30 days to submit a lien release. G.S. 45-36.9 starts that clock, and filing the release costs nothing.

If the lender misses that deadline, it is liable for your actual damages. You may also send a written demand by a trackable method. Should another 30 days go by after the lender receives it, the statute adds $1,000 plus reasonable attorney fees and costs. That right belongs to the landowner who made the demand and cannot be assigned.

Home equity lines and other future-advance loans need an extra step, because the creditor must also get a request to close the line. Ask the attorney to send that request along with the payoff letter, so the old lien does not stay on the record.

sections.h2: When a deed takes effect against others
sections.html:
A buyer whose deed is not yet registered in the county where the land sits has no protection against lien creditors or other purchasers. G.S. 47-18 extends that rule to contracts to convey, options, leases running longer than three years, and first-refusal rights.

Priority goes by the time of registration, which is why attorneys file the same day the money moves, tax paid first. Do not consider the sale done until you hold the recording confirmation.

  • Confirm who records the deed, and when.
  • Get the book and page, or document number, after it posts.
  • File the recorded release of your old loan with your closing papers.

County bills are due September 1 of the fiscal year and carry no interest if paid before January 6. Later payment triggers G.S. 105-360 interest of two percent, then three-fourths of one percent each month starting February 1.

The tax lien exists before the bill is mailed. G.S. 105-355 puts it on the parcel as of the listing date under G.S. 105-285, penalties and interest included, so title searchers look at tax status first.

How the year's tax is shared is a contract question. Pull the bill and its payment status from the county tax office, then have your attorney explain the split before you trust a net-proceeds estimate.

Ask for every deduction from your proceeds in writing, each with the reason for it. A single phone call before closing day heads off most surprises.

  • What price is the deed tax based on, and which county collects it?
  • What is the payoff amount, and who follows up on the lender's release?
  • Which filing charges are mine and which are the buyer's?
  • How does the contract split the property tax bill?
  • When will the deed be filed, and will you send the confirmation?

Bring a photo ID and your loan account number to the signing. Check that your name is spelled on the paperwork exactly as on your current deed, since a mismatch can stall things while the lawyer prepares a corrected one. Living elsewhere? Ask about signing early before a notary and where your proceeds will be wired.

Use the same checklist when you compare offers. Statutory items do not move with the buyer, so any gap between two offers traces back to contract terms.

sections.h2: Selling while the house is in foreclosure
sections.html:
Costs can shift, since a power-of-sale foreclosure leaves timing to the clerk of superior court and the upset bid process. Under G.S. 45-21.27, each upset bid must exceed the reported price or last bid by at least 5 percent and no less than $750, and the bidder posts a deposit of 5 percent, never below $750. Each new bid reopens a ten-day window.

A sale that closes before the foreclosure concludes removes that uncertainty, though the lender may have piled fees onto the payoff. Request an itemized statement in writing and pass it to the closing attorney immediately.

faqs.q: Who bears the deed tax on a North Carolina sale?
faqs.a: The seller, as transferor under G.S. 105-228.30. The closing lawyer typically deducts it from your proceeds.

faqs.q: Can I close without a lawyer in North Carolina?
faqs.a: Not realistically. Drafting a deed or reviewing title counts as practicing law under G.S. 84-2.1, with narrow room for a broker's preprinted form or a lease form.

faqs.q: What does filing my loan release cost?
faqs.a: It is free. G.S. 161-10 sets no fee for a satisfaction, and G.S. 45-36.9 gives the lender 30 days after payoff to file it.

faqs.q: What does the county charge to file a standard deed?
faqs.a: Under G.S. 161-10 the first 15 pages cost $26.00, and every page after that adds $4.00. A nonstandard document draws an added charge, so ask the office.

faqs.q: Where is the deed tax paid for land in two counties?
faqs.a: In whichever county holds more of the land's value. Have the attorney confirm which office takes the deed.
